data.q: What keyword is used to start a new goroutine in Go?
data.e: The `go` keyword launches a new goroutine. `thread`, `async`, and `spawn` are not Go keywords for this purpose.

data.q: Which statement correctly creates an unbuffered channel of type int?
data.e: `make(chan int)` creates an unbuffered channel. `make(chan int, 0)` also creates an unbuffered channel but is less idiomatic. `new` and composite literals are not used for channels.

data.q: What happens when you send to a nil channel?
data.e: Sending to a nil channel blocks forever. The same applies to receiving from a nil channel.

data.q: How do you close a channel in Go?
data.e: The built-in `close` function closes a channel. Channels do not have a `Close` method, and `delete` is for maps.

data.q: What is the result of receiving from a closed channel?
o: Returns the zero value and false
Returns the last sent value and true
data.e: Receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value of the channel's type and `false` as the second return value, indicating the channel is closed.

data.q: Which of the following is a valid use of the `select` statement?
data.e: `select` lets a goroutine wait on multiple communication operations (send/receive). It is not a switch, range, or close mechanism.

data.q: What does a buffered channel with capacity 3 allow?
o: Up to 3 sends without a corresponding receive
Only 3 total messages over the channel's lifetime
data.e: A buffered channel of capacity 3 can hold up to 3 values before sends block. Receives can happen anytime; the buffer does not limit total messages.

data.q: Which package provides synchronization primitives like WaitGroup and Mutex?
data.e: The `sync` package contains `WaitGroup`, `Mutex`, `RWMutex`, `Cond`, `Once`, and `Pool`. `sync/atomic` provides low-level atomic operations.

o: To wait for a collection of goroutines to finish
To protect shared memory from concurrent access
To limit the number of concurrent goroutines
data.e: `WaitGroup` waits for a group of goroutines to finish by calling `Add`, `Done`, and `Wait`. It does not provide mutual exclusion or signaling directly.

data.q: What happens if you call `wg.Add(1)` after `wg.Wait()` has been called on the same WaitGroup?
o: Blocks until the new goroutine finishes
Adds to the counter but Wait returns immediately
data.e: Calling `Add` with a positive value after `Wait` has returned (i.e., when the counter is zero) causes a panic. You must add before waiting.

data.q: Which statement about channel direction is correct?
o: chan<- int is a send-only channel type
<-chan int is a send-only channel type
Direction is enforced only at runtime
data.e: `chan<- int` denotes a send-only channel, `<-chan int` denotes receive-only. Direction is part of the type and checked at compile time.

o: Limits the program to a single OS thread for executing user-level code
Sets the maximum number of goroutines to 1
Forces all channels to be unbuffered
data.e: `GOMAXPROCS` sets the maximum number of OS threads that can execute user-level Go code simultaneously. It does not limit goroutine count or channel buffering.

data.q: How can you safely read from a channel until it is closed?
o: Both A and B are correct
data.e: Both `for v := range ch` and the manual `ok` check are idiomatic ways to read until a channel is closed. The range loop automatically handles the closed condition.

data.q: What does the `select` statement do when multiple cases are ready?
o: Executes the first case in lexical order
Blocks until only one case is ready
data.e: If multiple cases are ready, `select` picks one pseudo-randomly. It does not execute all, nor does it prioritize lexical order.

data.q: Which of the following will cause a deadlock?
o: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- 1 }(); <-ch
data.e: Sending to an unbuffered channel without a concurrent receiver blocks forever, causing a deadlock. The other examples either have a receiver, a buffer, or read from a closed channel (which returns immediately).

data.q: What is the zero value of a channel type?
data.e: The zero value of a channel is `nil`. A nil channel blocks on both send and receive indefinitely.
